GHSA-35pj-rg5r-8rpv.title: Daemon registry is briefly readable by other local users when it is created
GHSA-35pj-rg5r-8rpv.description: ### Impact A **Gradle client** (the `gradle`/`gradlew` CLI or an IDE using the Tooling API) finds running **Gradle daemons** through a registry file, `daemon/<Gradle version>/registry.bin` in the Gradle user home. For each daemon, the registry records its loopback address and the secret token that authenticates clients to it. Anyone holding a token can connect to that daemon and have it run a build as the user who started it. The registry is meant to be readable by its owner only. This advisory is about a vulnerability in how the registry file is created. When the first daemon of a given Gradle version starts, Gradle creates the version directory and the registry file with the default permissions of the process, which on most Linux and macOS systems let other users read them. Gradle restricts both to the owner right afterwards, then writes the registry content. Another local user who opens the registry file within that window keeps a handle to it that remains readable after the permissions change, and reads the daemon tokens written afterwards. Since the file is rewritten in place, the same handle also reads every later update, so the attacker obtains the token of every daemon of that Gradle version for as long as the file exists. With a token, the attacker can submit a build to the victim's daemon, which runs code with the privileges of the user running the build and exposes in-memory and on-disk secrets available to it. Builds running on **shared / multi-user build hosts** are the most at risk. The attacker must be able to traverse every directory down to the registry file. Gradle does not restrict the permissions of the Gradle user home when it creates it, so whether other users can reach it depends on the user's home directory and umask. A Gradle user home, or home directory, that other users cannot enter prevents the attack. The window only exists when the first daemon of a Gradle version starts in a given Gradle user home. This vulnerability is not exploitable from a remote network connection. ### Patches Gradle now creates the daemon registry and its directory with owner-only permissions in the call that creates them. There is no longer a window during which other users can open the registry. Each update of the daemon registry now atomically replaces the file with a new one instead of rewriting it in place. A handle opened on an earlier registry file does not read the tokens written afterwards. | Fix version | Availability | | ---------- | ----------- | | 9.9.2 | OSS | | 9.8.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.7.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.6.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.5.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.4.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.3.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.2.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 8.14.8 | OSS | | 7.6.9 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | ### Workarounds Upgrading Gradle is our recommended fix. If you cannot upgrade immediately: * **Make the Gradle user home accessible to its owner only.** Run `chmod 700 ~/.gradle`, or the same on the directory set by `GRADLE_USER_HOME`. Other users can then no longer reach the files Gradle creates inside it. * **Do not run builds on shared, multi-user machines.** Ensure only trusted users have local (same-host) access to a machine where Gradle builds run. On CI, prefer single-tenant, ephemeral runners rather than shared hosts. After upgrading or applying a workaround, stop the daemons with `gradle --stop` and delete the `registry.bin` files in `<Gradle user home>/daemon/`. A handle opened before the change keeps reading the file until it is replaced. ### Forensics A process of another user holding a registry file open indicates an attempt. On Linux and macOS, `lsof` lists the processes that have the files open: lsof <Gradle user home>/daemon/*/registry.bin Nothing in Gradle's output tells a build submitted with a stolen token apart from a legitimate one. The daemon log, `<Gradle user home>/daemon/<Gradle version>/daemon-<pid>.out.log`, records every build request the daemon receives, with the directory it was started from: `Received command: Build{id=<id>, currentDir=<directory>}.` An entry whose directory or time matches no build you ran indicates that someone else used the daemon. Gradle deletes daemon log files after 14 days by default. Documentation about daemon logs can be found [here](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/gradle_daemon.html#sec:daemon_logs). > [!IMPORTANT] > The lack of a log entry cannot be used to conclude no such attack was performed. The presence of a log entry is not a confirmation that an attack happened, but an indication that more investigations are needed. ### References * [Securing the Build Tool: Protect the Gradle User Home](https://docs.gradle.org/nightly/userguide/securing_build_tool.html#sec:user_home) * [Information disclosure through temporary directory permissions](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-fp8h-qmr5-j4c8) * [Gradle client trusts the content of the daemon registry](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-gqrr-4j89-5267) * [Daemon client trusts stale registry entries (port squatting)](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-pcp8-98xm-c6pr) More about this type of vulnerabilities: * https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/276.html * https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/362.html

GHSA-7f7r-77ff-fr6f.title: Transitive snapshot dependencies skip dependency verification
GHSA-7f7r-77ff-fr6f.description: ### Impact Gradle's [dependency verification](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html) checks every dependency and plugin a build downloads against checksums and trusted signing keys recorded in `gradle/verification-metadata.xml`. Once that file is written and reviewed, a build fails if a dependency is replaced by different content, for instance after a repository compromise. Changing modules, such as `-SNAPSHOT` versions, are [excluded](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html#sec:verification-scope) because their content changes by design. This advisory is about a vulnerability in dependency verification. The exclusion also applies to changing modules that a build does not declare itself, but reaches through the metadata of another dependency. When a release the build depends on declares a dependency on a `-SNAPSHOT` version, Gradle verifies the release but neither verifies the snapshot nor records anything for it when generating `verification-metadata.xml`. Reviewing the changes to that file does not reveal the snapshot. An attacker who publishes such a release, or who controls the coordinates of the snapshot it depends on, can serve harmless content while the release is reviewed and adopted, then replace the snapshot at any later time. Every later build resolves the new content without a verification failure. When the snapshot is on the classpath of a plugin or of build logic, or its code is run by a task such as tests, the attacker's code runs with the privileges of the user running the build. This exposes the secrets available to the build, including repository and publishing credentials. Only builds that use dependency verification are affected: a build without it does not verify any dependency, snapshot or not. Among those, builds that declare a repository serving snapshots, such as a snapshot repository, JitPack or an internal repository manager proxying one, are at risk. Maven Central does not serve snapshots, and Gradle does not use repositories declared in POM files, so a build resolving only from Maven Central is not exposed. The Gradle Plugin Portal does not support snapshots either: the content of a version published there cannot change, even when the version is named `-SNAPSHOT`, so plugins and dependencies resolved from it cannot be replaced this way. ### Patches With dependency verification enabled, Gradle now verifies changing modules like any other module, whether the build declares them itself or reaches them through another dependency. Their metadata and artifacts are checked against `verification-metadata.xml`, and `--write-verification-metadata` records them. This changes the behavior of builds that use dependency verification and resolve changing modules, including snapshots they declare themselves. Such a build fails with `Dependency verification failed` until its changing modules are covered by `verification-metadata.xml`. The checksum of a snapshot changes each time it is published, so prefer [verifying signatures](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html#sec:signature-verification) and trusting the keys that sign them. Snapshots you accept without verification must be [trusted explicitly](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html#sec:trusting-artifacts), which makes the exemption visible to reviewers of that file: ```xml <trusted-artifacts> <trust group='com.example' version='.*-SNAPSHOT' regex='true'/> </trusted-artifacts> ``` | Fix version | Availability | | ---------- | ----------- | | 9.9.2 | OSS | | 9.8.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.7.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.6.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.5.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.4.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.3.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.2.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 8.14.8 | OSS | | 7.6.9 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | ### Workarounds Upgrading Gradle is our recommended fix. If you cannot upgrade immediately: * **Fail the build on changing versions.** [`failOnChangingVersions()`](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/resolution_rules.html#sec:conflict-resolution-strategy) rejects changing modules anywhere in the dependency graph, including those brought in by other dependencies. Apply it to the build script classpath as well, for example in an init script: ```kotlin allprojects { configurations.configureEach { resolutionStrategy.failOnChangingVersions() } buildscript.configurations.configureEach { resolutionStrategy.failOnChangingVersions() } } ``` It cannot be combined with dependency locking on the same configuration. * **Restrict what snapshot repositories can serve.** Use [repository content filtering](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/filtering_repository_content.html) to limit each repository that serves snapshots to the groups you expect from it, and declare the other repositories with `mavenContent { releasesOnly() }`. ### Forensics Snapshots in the dependency graph are listed with a `-SNAPSHOT` version in the output of `gradle dependencies` and in build scans. `gradle dependencyInsight --dependency MODULE` shows which dependency brought a given snapshot in. The Gradle dependency cache keeps each downloaded file under `<Gradle user home>/caches/modules-2/files-2.1/<group>/<module>/<version>/<sha1>/`. Several `<sha1>` directories under a snapshot version show that its content changed over time. > [!IMPORTANT] > The lack of such traces cannot be used to conclude no such attack was performed. Their presence is not a confirmation that an attack happened, but an indication that more investigations are needed. ### References * [Verifying dependencies](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html) * [Filtering repository content](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/filtering_repository_content.html) More about this type of vulnerabilities: * https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/494.html * https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/829.html

GHSA-j5m7-59rp-24f5.title: Failure to disable repositories failing to establish an SSL connection can expose builds to malicious artifacts
GHSA-j5m7-59rp-24f5.description: ### Impact When resolving dependencies, Gradle searches repositories in declaration order. If it encounters connection errors, Gradle will disable the repository and fail dependency resolution. This is necessary for both reproducibility and security reasons to prevent dependencies from being resolved from other repositories without warning. In previous versions of Gradle, some exceptions were not treated as fatal errors and would not cause a repository to be disabled. If a build encountered one of these exceptions, Gradle would continue to the next repository in the list and potentially resolve dependencies from a different repository. #### Vulnerability caused by continuing after SSL connection establishment errors Exceptions like `SSLException` or `SSLHandshakeException` are neither handled as fatal exceptions nor as transient failures. Gradle should fail hard on any failure that is not transient, disable the repository and not move on to the next one. This behavior could allow an attacker to disrupt the service of a repository and leverage another repository to serve malicious artifacts. This attack requires the attacker to have control over a repository after the disrupted repository. ### Patches Gradle has introduced a change in behavior to stop searching other repositories when encountering these errors. | Fix version | Availability | | ---------- | ----------- | | 9.8.1 | OSS | | 9.7.2 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.6.2 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.5.2 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.4.2 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.3.2 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.2.2 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.1.1 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 8.14.6 | OSS | | 7.6.7 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | ### Workarounds If you are using strict [repository content filtering](https://docs.gradle.org/9.3.0/userguide/filtering_repository_content.html#header) and / or [dependency verification](https://docs.gradle.org/9.3.0/userguide/dependency_verification.html), your build is safe from the potential vulnerabilities described above. If you cannot update to a newer Gradle version, configuring [dependency verification](https://docs.gradle.org/9.3.0/userguide/dependency_verification.html) is the best way to make sure your build resolves the dependencies you expect and nothing else. You should also review which repositories your builds use to check for unused or outdated repository declarations. ### References * [Failure to disable repositories failing to answer can expose builds to malicious artifacts](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-mqwm-5m85-gmcv) More about this type of vulnerabilities: * https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/494.html * https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/829.html

GHSA-pcp8-98xm-c6pr.title: Daemon client trusts stale registry entries (port squatting)
GHSA-pcp8-98xm-c6pr.description: ### Impact A **Gradle client** (the `gradle`/`gradlew` CLI or an IDE using the Tooling API) looks up running **Gradle daemons** in a registry file under the Gradle user home, then connects to an idle daemon over a loopback TCP connection and sends it the build to run. The client authenticates itself to the daemon with a secret token, but the daemon is not authenticated to the client, and the client does not check that the daemon process recorded in the registry is still running. This advisory is about a vulnerability on this communication channel. When a daemon terminates without removing itself from the registry, for example when it is killed with `kill -9`, stopped by the out-of-memory killer or crashes, its loopback port becomes free while the registry still points to it. Another local user who binds that port receives the next build request from the victim's client. That request contains the client's environment variables, system properties and standard input, which commonly hold credentials and CI tokens. The attacker can then answer with crafted messages that the client deserializes: * in an IDE or any other Tooling API client, a crafted reply makes the client process load and run code from a jar chosen by the attacker; * on the command line, deserializing a hostile object graph can lead to code execution in the client, depending on the classes available, or to a denial of service. Code execution in the client runs with the privileges of the user running the build. This has been demonstrated with a proof-of-concept. This advisory does not publish the proof-of-concept. Builds running on **shared / multi-user build hosts** are the most at risk. The vulnerability requires a daemon to have terminated abnormally, leaving a stale entry in the registry, and the attacker to listen on that daemon's port when the victim next starts a build or synchronizes a project in an IDE. This vulnerability is not exploitable from a remote network connection. ### Patches The client and the daemon now authenticate each other as soon as a connection opens, before any message is exchanged. The connection token in the registry holds two secrets. The client proves it holds the first one, and only then does the daemon answer with the second. The client checks that answer before it sends anything else. A process listening on the port of a terminated daemon cannot produce the daemon's secret. The client therefore drops the connection, removes the stale entry from the registry, and uses or starts another daemon. That process only receives the client's half of the token of a daemon that no longer exists. The fix depends on the Gradle version used by the build, not on the Tooling API version of the IDE. | Fix version | Availability | | ---------- | ----------- | | 9.9.1 | OSS | | 9.8.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.7.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.6.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.5.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.4.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.3.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.2.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 8.14.7 | OSS | | 7.6.8 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | ### Workarounds Upgrading Gradle is our recommended fix. If you cannot upgrade immediately: * **Do not run builds on shared, multi-user machines.** Ensure only trusted users have local (same-host) access to a machine where Gradle builds run. On CI, prefer single-tenant, ephemeral runners rather than shared hosts. The attacker must be a co-located local principal to gain access to the Gradle build. * **Clear the daemon registry after a daemon terminated abnormally, before the next build.** Delete `<Gradle user home>/daemon/<Gradle version>/registry.bin`. This is safe while daemons are running. Clients no longer find the running daemons and start new ones, and the unregistered daemons stop after their idle timeout (3 hours by default). On an affected version, do not use `gradle --status` or `gradle --stop` for this: both connect to every daemon in the registry, including stale entries. If you cannot apply these mitigations, restrict which users and processes share a host with your builds until you can upgrade. ### Forensics Gradle's output does not tell a process squatting a daemon's port apart from a daemon whose port is free. Look for the conditions of the attack on the build host instead: * A daemon that terminated abnormally leaves a log file, `<Gradle user home>/daemon/<Gradle version>/daemon-<pid>.out.log`, that does not end with `Daemon vm is shutting down...` even though process `<pid>` is no longer running. Its port is on the line `Daemon starting at: …, with address: [… port:<port>, …]`. * A process of another user listening on that port indicates an attempt. On Linux and macOS: `lsof -nP -iTCP:<port> -sTCP:LISTEN`. > [!IMPORTANT] > These checks reveal the conditions for the attack, not the attack itself: by default, Gradle does not record which process a client sent its request to. Daemons also terminate abnormally for ordinary reasons, such as the out-of-memory killer, a crash or a machine reboot, so a log file without a shutdown line is not evidence of an attack. A squatting process only shows while it is still listening, and Gradle deletes daemon log files after 14 days by default, so finding neither does not rule out an attack. ### References * [Deserialization of untrusted Java objects before authentication in the client - daemon communication](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-xwqc-3h47-hg64) * [Project-controlled daemon registry location](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-gqrr-4j89-5267) * [Gradle architecture standard ADR-0002](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/blob/master/architecture/standards/0002-avoid-using-java-serialization.md), 'Avoid using Java serialization' — Gradle's own guidance to move off Java serialization, citing deserialization security among the reasons. * [JEP 290: Filter Incoming Serialization Data](https://openjdk.org/jeps/290) More about this type of vulnerabilities: * https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/287.html * https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/502.html

GHSA-7f7r-77ff-fr6f.description: ### Impact Gradle's [dependency verification](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html) checks every dependency and plugin a build downloads against checksums and trusted signing keys recorded in `gradle/verification-metadata.xml`. Once that file is written and reviewed, a build fails if a dependency is replaced by different content, for instance after a repository compromise. Changing modules, such as `-SNAPSHOT` versions, are [excluded](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html#sec:verification-scope) because their content changes by design. When a release the build depends on declares a dependency on a `-SNAPSHOT` version, Gradle verifies the release but neither verifies the snapshot nor records anything for it when generating `verification-metadata.xml`. Reviewing the changes to that file does not reveal the snapshot. An attacker who publishes such a release, or who controls the coordinates of the snapshot it depends on, can serve harmless content while the release is reviewed and adopted, then replace the snapshot at any later time. Every later build resolves the new content without a verification failure. When the snapshot is on the classpath of a plugin or of build logic, or its code is run by a task such as tests, the attacker's code runs with the privileges of the user running the build. This exposes the secrets available to the build, including repository and publishing credentials. Only builds that use dependency verification are affected: a build without it does not verify any dependency, snapshot or not. GHSA-j5m7-59rp-24f5.description: ### Impact When resolving dependencies, Gradle searches repositories in declaration order. If it encounters connection errors, Gradle will disable the repository and fail dependency resolution. This is necessary for both reproducibility and security reasons to prevent dependencies from being resolved from other repositories without warning. GHSA-pcp8-98xm-c6pr.title: Daemon client trusts stale registry entries (port squatting)
GHSA-pcp8-98xm-c6pr.description: ### Impact A **Gradle client** (the `gradle`/`gradlew` CLI or an IDE using the Tooling API) looks up running **Gradle daemons** in a registry file under the Gradle user home, then connects to an idle daemon over a loopback TCP connection and sends it the build to run. The client authenticates itself to the daemon with a secret token, but the daemon is not authenticated to the client, and the client does not check that the daemon process recorded in the registry is still running. This advisory is about a vulnerability on this communication channel. When a daemon terminates without removing itself from the registry, for example when it is killed with `kill -9`, stopped by the out-of-memory killer or crashes, its loopback port becomes free while the registry still points to it. Another local user who binds that port receives the next build request from the victim's client. That request contains the client's environment variables, system properties and standard input, which commonly hold credentials and CI tokens. The attacker can then answer with crafted messages that the client deserializes: * in an IDE or any other Tooling API client, a crafted reply makes the client process load and run code from a jar chosen by the attacker; * on the command line, deserializing a hostile object graph can lead to code execution in the client, depending on the classes available, or to a denial of service. Code execution in the client runs with the privileges of the user running the build. This has been demonstrated with a proof-of-concept. This advisory does not publish the proof-of-concept. Builds running on **shared / multi-user build hosts** are the most at risk. The vulnerability requires a daemon to have terminated abnormally, leaving a stale entry in the registry, and the attacker to listen on that daemon's port when the victim next starts a build or synchronizes a project in an IDE. This vulnerability is not exploitable from a remote network connection. ### Patches The client and the daemon now authenticate each other as soon as a connection opens, before any message is exchanged. The connection token in the registry holds two secrets. The client proves it holds the first one, and only then does the daemon answer with the second. The client checks that answer before it sends anything else. A process listening on the port of a terminated daemon cannot produce the daemon's secret. The client therefore drops the connection, removes the stale entry from the registry, and uses or starts another daemon. That process only receives the client's half of the token of a daemon that no longer exists. The fix depends on the Gradle version used by the build, not on the Tooling API version of the IDE. | Fix version | Availability | | ---------- | ----------- | | 9.9.1 | OSS | | 9.8.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.7.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.6.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.5.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.4.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.3.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.2.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 8.14.7 | OSS | | 7.6.8 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | ### Workarounds Upgrading Gradle is our recommended fix. If you cannot upgrade immediately: * **Do not run builds on shared, multi-user machines.** Ensure only trusted users have local (same-host) access to a machine where Gradle builds run. On CI, prefer single-tenant, ephemeral runners rather than shared hosts. The attacker must be a co-located local principal to gain access to the Gradle build. * **Clear the daemon registry after a daemon terminated abnormally, before the next build.** Delete `<Gradle user home>/daemon/<Gradle version>/registry.bin`. This is safe while daemons are running. Clients no longer find the running daemons and start new ones, and the unregistered daemons stop after their idle timeout (3 hours by default). On an affected version, do not use `gradle --status` or `gradle --stop` for this: both connect to every daemon in the registry, including stale entries. If you cannot apply these mitigations, restrict which users and processes share a host with your builds until you can upgrade. ### Forensics Gradle's output does not tell a process squatting a daemon's port apart from a daemon whose port is free. Look for the conditions of the attack on the build host instead: * A daemon that terminated abnormally leaves a log file, `<Gradle user home>/daemon/<Gradle version>/daemon-<pid>.out.log`, that does not end with `Daemon vm is shutting down...` even though process `<pid>` is no longer running. Its port is on the line `Daemon starting at: …, with address: [… port:<port>, …]`. * A process of another user listening on that port indicates an attempt. On Linux and macOS: `lsof -nP -iTCP:<port> -sTCP:LISTEN`. > [!IMPORTANT] > These checks reveal the conditions for the attack, not the attack itself: by default, Gradle does not record which process a client sent its request to. A squatting process only shows while it is still listening, and Gradle deletes daemon log files after 14 days by default, so finding neither does not rule out an attack. ### References * [Deserialization of untrusted Java objects before authentication in the client - daemon communication](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-xwqc-3h47-hg64) * [Project-controlled daemon registry location](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-gqrr-4j89-5267) * [Gradle architecture standard ADR-0002](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/blob/master/architecture/standards/0002-avoid-using-java-serialization.md), 'Avoid using Java serialization' — Gradle's own guidance to move off Java serialization, citing deserialization security among the reasons. * [JEP 290: Filter Incoming Serialization Data](https://openjdk.org/jeps/290) More about this type of vulnerabilities: * https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/287.html * https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/502.html

GHSA-pcp8-98xm-c6pr.description: ### Impact A **Gradle client** (the `gradle`/`gradlew` CLI or an IDE using the Tooling API) looks up running **Gradle daemons** in a registry file under the Gradle user home, then connects to an idle daemon over a loopback TCP connection and sends it the build to run. This advisory is about a vulnerability on this communication channel. When a daemon terminates without removing itself from the registry, for example when it is killed with `kill -9`, stopped by the out-of-memory killer or crashes, its loopback port becomes free while the registry still points to it. Another local user who binds that port receives the next build request from the victim's client. That request contains the client's environment variables, system properties and standard input, which commonly hold credentials and CI tokens. The attacker can then answer with crafted messages that the client deserializes: * in an IDE or any other Tooling API client, a crafted reply makes the client process load and run code from a jar chosen by the attacker; * on the command line, deserializing a hostile object graph can lead to code execution in the client, depending on the classes available, or to a denial of service. Code execution in the client runs with the privileges of the user running the build. This has been demonstrated with a proof-of-concept. This advisory does not publish the proof-of-concept. Builds running on **shared / multi-user build hosts** are the most at risk. The vulnerability requires a daemon to have terminated abnormally, leaving a stale entry in the registry, and the attacker to listen on that daemon's port when the victim next starts a build or synchronizes a project in an IDE. This vulnerability is not exploitable from a remote network connection. ### Patches The client and the daemon now authenticate each other as soon as a connection opens, before any message is exchanged. The connection token in the registry holds two secrets. The client proves it holds the first one, and only then does the daemon answer with the second. The client checks that answer before it sends anything else. A process listening on the port of a terminated daemon cannot produce the daemon's secret. The client therefore drops the connection, removes the stale entry from the registry, and uses or starts another daemon. GHSA-7f7r-77ff-fr6f.title: Transitive snapshot dependencies skip dependency verification
GHSA-7f7r-77ff-fr6f.description: ### Impact Gradle's [dependency verification](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html) checks every dependency and plugin a build downloads against checksums and trusted signing keys recorded in `gradle/verification-metadata.xml`. Once that file is written and reviewed, a build fails if a dependency is replaced by different content, for instance after a repository compromise. Changing modules, such as `-SNAPSHOT` versions, are [excluded](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html#sec:verification-scope) because their content changes by design. This advisory is about a vulnerability in dependency verification. The exclusion also applies to changing modules that a build does not declare itself, but reaches through the metadata of another dependency. When a release the build depends on declares a dependency on a `-SNAPSHOT` version, Gradle verifies the release but neither verifies the snapshot nor records anything for it when generating `verification-metadata.xml`. Reviewing the changes to that file does not reveal the snapshot. An attacker who publishes such a release, or who controls the coordinates of the snapshot it depends on, can serve harmless content while the release is reviewed and adopted, then replace the snapshot at any later time. Every later build resolves the new content without a verification failure. When the snapshot is on the classpath of a plugin or of build logic, or its code is run by a task such as tests, the attacker's code runs with the privileges of the user running the build. This exposes the secrets available to the build, including repository and publishing credentials. Only builds that use dependency verification are affected: a build without it does not verify any dependency, snapshot or not. Maven Central does not serve snapshots, and Gradle does not use repositories declared in POM files, so a build resolving only from Maven Central is not exposed. The Gradle Plugin Portal does not support snapshots either: the content of a version published there cannot change, even when the version is named `-SNAPSHOT`, so plugins and dependencies resolved from it cannot be replaced this way. ### Patches With dependency verification enabled, Gradle now verifies changing modules like any other module, whether the build declares them itself or reaches them through another dependency. This changes the behavior of builds that use dependency verification and resolve changing modules, including snapshots they declare themselves. Such a build fails with `Dependency verification failed` until its changing modules are covered by `verification-metadata.xml`. Snapshots you accept without verification must be [trusted explicitly](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html#sec:trusting-artifacts), which makes the exemption visible to reviewers of that file: ```xml <trusted-artifacts> <trust group='com.example' version='.*-SNAPSHOT' regex='true'/> </trusted-artifacts> ``` | Fix version | Availability | | ---------- | ----------- | | 9.9.2 | OSS | | 9.8.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.7.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.6.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.5.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.4.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.3.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.2.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 8.14.8 | OSS | | 7.6.9 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | ### Workarounds Upgrading Gradle is our recommended fix. If you cannot upgrade immediately: * **Fail the build on changing versions.** [`failOnChangingVersions()`](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/resolution_rules.html#sec:conflict-resolution-strategy) rejects changing modules anywhere in the dependency graph, including those brought in by other dependencies. Apply it to the build script classpath as well, for example in an init script: ```kotlin allprojects { configurations.configureEach { resolutionStrategy.failOnChangingVersions() } buildscript.configurations.configureEach { resolutionStrategy.failOnChangingVersions() } } ``` It cannot be combined with dependency locking on the same configuration. * **Restrict what snapshot repositories can serve.** Use [repository content filtering](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/filtering_repository_content.html) to limit each repository that serves snapshots to the groups you expect from it, and declare the other repositories with `mavenContent { releasesOnly() }`. ### Forensics Snapshots in the dependency graph are listed with a `-SNAPSHOT` version in the output of `gradle dependencies` and in build scans. `gradle dependencyInsight --dependency MODULE` shows which dependency brought a given snapshot in. The Gradle dependency cache keeps each downloaded file under `<Gradle user home>/caches/modules-2/files-2.1/<group>/<module>/<version>/<sha1>/`. Several `<sha1>` directories under a snapshot version show that its content changed over time. > [!IMPORTANT] > The lack of such traces cannot be used to conclude no such attack was performed. Their presence is not a confirmation that an attack happened, but an indication that more investigations are needed. ### References * [Verifying dependencies](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html) * [Filtering repository content](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/filtering_repository_content.html) More about this type of vulnerabilities: * https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/494.html * https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/829.html

GHSA-35pj-rg5r-8rpv.title: Daemon registry is briefly readable by other local users when it is created
GHSA-35pj-rg5r-8rpv.description: ### Impact A **Gradle client** (the `gradle`/`gradlew` CLI or an IDE using the Tooling API) finds running **Gradle daemons** through a registry file, `daemon/<Gradle version>/registry.bin` in the Gradle user home. For each daemon, the registry records its loopback address and the secret token that authenticates clients to it. Anyone holding a token can connect to that daemon and have it run a build as the user who started it. The registry is meant to be readable by its owner only. This advisory is about a vulnerability in how the registry file is created. When the first daemon of a given Gradle version starts, Gradle creates the version directory and the registry file with the default permissions of the process, which on most Linux and macOS systems let other users read them. Gradle restricts both to the owner right afterwards, then writes the registry content. Another local user who opens the registry file within that window keeps a handle to it that remains readable after the permissions change, and reads the daemon tokens written afterwards. Since the file is rewritten in place, the same handle also reads every later update, so the attacker obtains the token of every daemon of that Gradle version for as long as the file exists. With a token, the attacker can submit a build to the victim's daemon, which runs code with the privileges of the user running the build and exposes in-memory and on-disk secrets available to it. Builds running on **shared / multi-user build hosts** are the most at risk. The attacker must be able to traverse every directory down to the registry file. Gradle does not restrict the permissions of the Gradle user home when it creates it, so whether other users can reach it depends on the user's home directory and umask. A Gradle user home, or home directory, that other users cannot enter prevents the attack. The window only exists when the first daemon of a Gradle version starts in a given Gradle user home. This vulnerability is not exploitable from a remote network connection. ### Patches Gradle now creates the daemon registry and its directory with owner-only permissions in the call that creates them. There is no longer a window during which other users can open the registry. Each update of the daemon registry now atomically replaces the file with a new one instead of rewriting it in place. A handle opened on an earlier registry file does not read the tokens written afterwards. | Fix version | Availability | | ---------- | ----------- | | 9.9.2 | OSS | | 9.8.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.7.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.6.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.5.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.4.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.3.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.2.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 8.14.8 | OSS | | 7.6.9 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | ### Workarounds Upgrading Gradle is our recommended fix. If you cannot upgrade immediately: * **Make the Gradle user home accessible to its owner only.** Run `chmod 700 ~/.gradle`, or the same on the directory set by `GRADLE_USER_HOME`. Other users can then no longer reach the files Gradle creates inside it. * **Do not run builds on shared, multi-user machines.** Ensure only trusted users have local (same-host) access to a machine where Gradle builds run. On CI, prefer single-tenant, ephemeral runners rather than shared hosts. After upgrading or applying a workaround, stop the daemons with `gradle --stop` and delete the `registry.bin` files in `<Gradle user home>/daemon/`. A handle opened before the change keeps reading the file until it is replaced. ### Forensics A process of another user holding a registry file open indicates an attempt. On Linux and macOS, `lsof` lists the processes that have the files open: lsof <Gradle user home>/daemon/*/registry.bin Nothing in Gradle's output tells a build submitted with a stolen token apart from a legitimate one. The daemon log, `<Gradle user home>/daemon/<Gradle version>/daemon-<pid>.out.log`, records every build request the daemon receives, with the directory it was started from: `Received command: Build{id=<id>, currentDir=<directory>}.` An entry whose directory or time matches no build you ran indicates that someone else used the daemon. Gradle deletes daemon log files after 14 days by default. Documentation about daemon logs can be found [here](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/gradle_daemon.html#sec:daemon_logs). > [!IMPORTANT] > The lack of a log entry cannot be used to conclude no such attack was performed. The presence of a log entry is not a confirmation that an attack happened, but an indication that more investigations are needed. ### References * [Securing the Build Tool: Protect the Gradle User Home](https://docs.gradle.org/nightly/userguide/securing_build_tool.html#sec:user_home) * [Information disclosure through temporary directory permissions](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-fp8h-qmr5-j4c8) * [Gradle client trusts the content of the daemon registry](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-gqrr-4j89-5267) * [Daemon client trusts stale registry entries (port squatting)](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-pcp8-98xm-c6pr) More about this type of vulnerabilities: * https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/276.html * https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/362.html

GHSA-7f7r-77ff-fr6f.title: Transitive snapshot dependencies skip dependency verification
GHSA-7f7r-77ff-fr6f.description: ### Impact Gradle's [dependency verification](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html) checks every dependency and plugin a build downloads against checksums and trusted signing keys recorded in `gradle/verification-metadata.xml`. Once that file is written and reviewed, a build fails if a dependency is replaced by different content, for instance after a repository compromise. Changing modules, such as `-SNAPSHOT` versions, are [excluded](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html#sec:verification-scope) because their content changes by design. This advisory is about a vulnerability in dependency verification. The exclusion also applies to changing modules that a build does not declare itself, but reaches through the metadata of another dependency. When a release the build depends on declares a dependency on a `-SNAPSHOT` version, Gradle verifies the release but neither verifies the snapshot nor records anything for it when generating `verification-metadata.xml`. Reviewing the changes to that file does not reveal the snapshot. An attacker who publishes such a release, or who controls the coordinates of the snapshot it depends on, can serve harmless content while the release is reviewed and adopted, then replace the snapshot at any later time. Every later build resolves the new content without a verification failure. When the snapshot is on the classpath of a plugin or of build logic, or its code is run by a task such as tests, the attacker's code runs with the privileges of the user running the build. This exposes the secrets available to the build, including repository and publishing credentials. Only builds that use dependency verification are affected: a build without it does not verify any dependency, snapshot or not. Among those, builds that declare a repository serving snapshots, such as a snapshot repository, JitPack or an internal repository manager proxying one, are at risk. Maven Central does not serve snapshots, and Gradle does not use repositories declared in POM files, so a build resolving only from Maven Central is not exposed. The Gradle Plugin Portal does not support snapshots either: the content of a version published there cannot change, even when the version is named `-SNAPSHOT`, so plugins and dependencies resolved from it cannot be replaced this way. ### Patches With dependency verification enabled, Gradle now verifies changing modules like any other module, whether the build declares them itself or reaches them through another dependency. Their metadata and artifacts are checked against `verification-metadata.xml`, and `--write-verification-metadata` records them. This changes the behavior of builds that use dependency verification and resolve changing modules, including snapshots they declare themselves. Such a build fails with `Dependency verification failed` until its changing modules are covered by `verification-metadata.xml`. The checksum of a snapshot changes each time it is published, so prefer [verifying signatures](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html#sec:signature-verification) and trusting the keys that sign them. Snapshots you accept without verification must be [trusted explicitly](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html#sec:trusting-artifacts), which makes the exemption visible to reviewers of that file: ```xml <trusted-artifacts> <trust group='com.example' version='.*-SNAPSHOT' regex='true'/> </trusted-artifacts> ``` | Fix version | Availability | | ---------- | ----------- | | 9.9.2 | OSS | | 9.8.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.7.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.6.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.5.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.4.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.3.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.2.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 8.14.8 | OSS | | 7.6.9 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | ### Workarounds Upgrading Gradle is our recommended fix. If you cannot upgrade immediately: * **Fail the build on changing versions.** [`failOnChangingVersions()`](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/resolution_rules.html#sec:conflict-resolution-strategy) rejects changing modules anywhere in the dependency graph, including those brought in by other dependencies. Apply it to the build script classpath as well, for example in an init script: ```kotlin allprojects { configurations.configureEach { resolutionStrategy.failOnChangingVersions() } buildscript.configurations.configureEach { resolutionStrategy.failOnChangingVersions() } } ``` It cannot be combined with dependency locking on the same configuration. * **Restrict what snapshot repositories can serve.** Use [repository content filtering](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/filtering_repository_content.html) to limit each repository that serves snapshots to the groups you expect from it, and declare the other repositories with `mavenContent { releasesOnly() }`. ### Forensics Snapshots in the dependency graph are listed with a `-SNAPSHOT` version in the output of `gradle dependencies` and in build scans. `gradle dependencyInsight --dependency MODULE` shows which dependency brought a given snapshot in. The Gradle dependency cache keeps each downloaded file under `<Gradle user home>/caches/modules-2/files-2.1/<group>/<module>/<version>/<sha1>/`. Several `<sha1>` directories under a snapshot version show that its content changed over time. > [!IMPORTANT] > The lack of such traces cannot be used to conclude no such attack was performed. Their presence is not a confirmation that an attack happened, but an indication that more investigations are needed. ### References * [Verifying dependencies](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html) * [Filtering repository content](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/filtering_repository_content.html) More about this type of vulnerabilities: * https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/494.html * https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/829.html

GHSA-j5m7-59rp-24f5.title: Failure to disable repositories failing to establish an SSL connection can expose builds to malicious artifacts
GHSA-j5m7-59rp-24f5.description: ### Impact When resolving dependencies, Gradle searches repositories in declaration order. If it encounters connection errors, Gradle will disable the repository and fail dependency resolution. This is necessary for both reproducibility and security reasons to prevent dependencies from being resolved from other repositories without warning. In previous versions of Gradle, some exceptions were not treated as fatal errors and would not cause a repository to be disabled. If a build encountered one of these exceptions, Gradle would continue to the next repository in the list and potentially resolve dependencies from a different repository. #### Vulnerability caused by continuing after SSL connection establishment errors Exceptions like `SSLException` or `SSLHandshakeException` are neither handled as fatal exceptions nor as transient failures. Gradle should fail hard on any failure that is not transient, disable the repository and not move on to the next one. This behavior could allow an attacker to disrupt the service of a repository and leverage another repository to serve malicious artifacts. This attack requires the attacker to have control over a repository after the disrupted repository. ### Patches Gradle has introduced a change in behavior to stop searching other repositories when encountering these errors. | Fix version | Availability | | ---------- | ----------- | | 9.8.1 | OSS | | 9.7.2 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.6.2 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.5.2 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.4.2 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.3.2 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.2.2 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.1.1 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 8.14.6 | OSS | | 7.6.7 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | ### Workarounds If you are using strict [repository content filtering](https://docs.gradle.org/9.3.0/userguide/filtering_repository_content.html#header) and / or [dependency verification](https://docs.gradle.org/9.3.0/userguide/dependency_verification.html), your build is safe from the potential vulnerabilities described above. If you cannot update to a newer Gradle version, configuring [dependency verification](https://docs.gradle.org/9.3.0/userguide/dependency_verification.html) is the best way to make sure your build resolves the dependencies you expect and nothing else. You should also review which repositories your builds use to check for unused or outdated repository declarations. ### References * [Failure to disable repositories failing to answer can expose builds to malicious artifacts](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-mqwm-5m85-gmcv) More about this type of vulnerabilities: * https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/494.html * https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/829.html

GHSA-pcp8-98xm-c6pr.title: Daemon client trusts stale registry entries (port squatting)
GHSA-pcp8-98xm-c6pr.description: ### Impact A **Gradle client** (the `gradle`/`gradlew` CLI or an IDE using the Tooling API) looks up running **Gradle daemons** in a registry file under the Gradle user home, then connects to an idle daemon over a loopback TCP connection and sends it the build to run. The client authenticates itself to the daemon with a secret token, but the daemon is not authenticated to the client, and the client does not check that the daemon process recorded in the registry is still running. This advisory is about a vulnerability on this communication channel. When a daemon terminates without removing itself from the registry, for example when it is killed with `kill -9`, stopped by the out-of-memory killer or crashes, its loopback port becomes free while the registry still points to it. Another local user who binds that port receives the next build request from the victim's client. That request contains the client's environment variables, system properties and standard input, which commonly hold credentials and CI tokens. The attacker can then answer with crafted messages that the client deserializes: * in an IDE or any other Tooling API client, a crafted reply makes the client process load and run code from a jar chosen by the attacker; * on the command line, deserializing a hostile object graph can lead to code execution in the client, depending on the classes available, or to a denial of service. Code execution in the client runs with the privileges of the user running the build. This has been demonstrated with a proof-of-concept. This advisory does not publish the proof-of-concept. Builds running on **shared / multi-user build hosts** are the most at risk. The vulnerability requires a daemon to have terminated abnormally, leaving a stale entry in the registry, and the attacker to listen on that daemon's port when the victim next starts a build or synchronizes a project in an IDE. This vulnerability is not exploitable from a remote network connection. ### Patches The client and the daemon now authenticate each other as soon as a connection opens, before any message is exchanged. The connection token in the registry holds two secrets. The client proves it holds the first one, and only then does the daemon answer with the second. The client checks that answer before it sends anything else. A process listening on the port of a terminated daemon cannot produce the daemon's secret. The client therefore drops the connection, removes the stale entry from the registry, and uses or starts another daemon. That process only receives the client's half of the token of a daemon that no longer exists. The fix depends on the Gradle version used by the build, not on the Tooling API version of the IDE. | Fix version | Availability | | ---------- | ----------- | | 9.9.1 | OSS | | 9.8.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.7.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.6.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.5.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.4.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.3.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 9.2.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | | 8.14.7 | OSS | | 7.6.8 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) | ### Workarounds Upgrading Gradle is our recommended fix. If you cannot upgrade immediately: * **Do not run builds on shared, multi-user machines.** Ensure only trusted users have local (same-host) access to a machine where Gradle builds run. On CI, prefer single-tenant, ephemeral runners rather than shared hosts. The attacker must be a co-located local principal to gain access to the Gradle build. * **Clear the daemon registry after a daemon terminated abnormally, before the next build.** Delete `<Gradle user home>/daemon/<Gradle version>/registry.bin`. This is safe while daemons are running. Clients no longer find the running daemons and start new ones, and the unregistered daemons stop after their idle timeout (3 hours by default). On an affected version, do not use `gradle --status` or `gradle --stop` for this: both connect to every daemon in the registry, including stale entries. If you cannot apply these mitigations, restrict which users and processes share a host with your builds until you can upgrade. ### Forensics Gradle's output does not tell a process squatting a daemon's port apart from a daemon whose port is free. Look for the conditions of the attack on the build host instead: * A daemon that terminated abnormally leaves a log file, `<Gradle user home>/daemon/<Gradle version>/daemon-<pid>.out.log`, that does not end with `Daemon vm is shutting down...` even though process `<pid>` is no longer running. Its port is on the line `Daemon starting at: …, with address: [… port:<port>, …]`. * A process of another user listening on that port indicates an attempt. On Linux and macOS: `lsof -nP -iTCP:<port> -sTCP:LISTEN`. > [!IMPORTANT] > These checks reveal the conditions for the attack, not the attack itself: by default, Gradle does not record which process a client sent its request to. Daemons also terminate abnormally for ordinary reasons, such as the out-of-memory killer, a crash or a machine reboot, so a log file without a shutdown line is not evidence of an attack. A squatting process only shows while it is still listening, and Gradle deletes daemon log files after 14 days by default, so finding neither does not rule out an attack. ### References * [Deserialization of untrusted Java objects before authentication in the client - daemon communication](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-xwqc-3h47-hg64) * [Project-controlled daemon registry location](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-gqrr-4j89-5267) * [Gradle architecture standard ADR-0002](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/blob/master/architecture/standards/0002-avoid-using-java-serialization.md), 'Avoid using Java serialization' — Gradle's own guidance to move off Java serialization, citing deserialization security among the reasons. * [JEP 290: Filter Incoming Serialization Data](https://openjdk.org/jeps/290) More about this type of vulnerabilities: * https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/287.html * https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/502.html
